issues.item: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
issues.explanation: This item is not a maladaptive strategy in the same format as the other items; it describes a trigger/reminder rather than the patient's coping response. Within the profile, the maladaptive strategies node otherwise contains actual strategies ('compulsive cleaning', 'positive reframing'), so this item is internally incoherent as a strategy selection.

vignette:
Layla

Layla was thirty-four when she walked into the clinic on a Tuesday afternoon, her hands folded tightly in her lap. She had come alone, which she preferred. Her ex-husband had stopped asking her to do things together nearly two years ago, after she had refused to attend his sister's wedding. She had not offered an explanation then, and she did not offer one now to the therapist. But the refusal had been the beginning of the end, or perhaps merely the visible moment when what had already broken finally split apart.

The trauma itself belonged to six years earlier, when Layla was still living in the small agricultural community in California's Central Valley where she had grown up. She worked in the packing sheds then, as she did now, sorting and boxing stone fruit alongside twenty other workers in the predawn hours. It was a job that required little conversation and paid enough. On a morning in late August, a coworker named Hassan had not shown up. By noon, the police had come to the shed. Hassan's wife had called them that morning. They had found him in their garage with a rope around his neck. He had been dead for hours—perhaps since before dawn, when Layla had been driving to work in the dark, listening to the radio.

She had known Hassan for seven years. They had shared lunch sometimes. He had two children, a boy and a girl. She learned later that his wife had been having an affair, that Hassan had discovered text messages on her phone the night before. The shed supervisor told her this in a low voice, as if it explained something. Layla had not asked for an explanation. What she could not stop seeing was Hassan's face as it had been on the morning he died—except she had not seen his face that morning, and this was the problem. She could only imagine it. She imagined it constantly.

The first months after his death, Layla had continued working. She had gone to the funeral, though she had not wanted to. She had sat in the back and watched Hassan's children sit in the front row, his daughter leaning against her mother, his son staring at nothing. Then something had shifted. She began to notice the way people looked at each other in the shed. She began to watch for signs—a man standing too close to someone else's wife, a woman laughing too hard at a coworker's joke. She had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that beneath the surface of ordinary interactions, terrible things were happening. She was certain now that the world was far more fragile than she had understood, that the people around her were capable of sudden, irreversible destruction.

The sound of babies crying had started to trigger something in her around that time. She did not fully understand why. Perhaps it was because Hassan's daughter had cried at the funeral. Perhaps it was because she associated the sound with loss, with children who would grow up without a father because of a decision made in a garage at night. Whatever the reason, when she heard a baby cry now—in a grocery store, in a neighbor's yard, sometimes even in dreams—she felt a surge of panic that she could not name.

Certain conversations had also become dangerous. If people began talking about relationships, about infidelity, about despair, she felt the urge to leave the room. She had developed a habit of excusing herself from work breaks when conversations turned in those directions. Her coworkers had begun to notice her isolation, though none of them had asked about it directly.

At home, she had developed rituals. She cleaned obsessively—her small apartment gleamed, every surface organized, every corner controlled. The act of cleaning was the only thing that quieted the static in her mind, the only thing that made her feel as though she had some purchase on the world. She also forced herself to think positive thoughts, to reject any idea that was dark or frightening. When images of Hassan came to her, she pushed them away violently, refusing to let them settle in her consciousness. But the pushing only created more pressure, more static.

Her marriage had deteriorated slowly under the weight of these habits. Her ex-husband had wanted to know why she was always cleaning, why she would not talk about certain things, why she seemed to be disappearing. She could not explain it to him because she could not explain it to herself. She only knew that people were not to be trusted, that she no longer belonged in the world she had known, and that the only safe place was inside her own controlled space.

Now, six years later, she was sitting in a therapist's office because her doctor had insisted. She was exhausted. The cleaning was taking four hours a day. She had called in sick to work twice in the past month because she could not face the shed, could not face the possibility of overhearing a conversation that would send her spiraling. She was losing income. She was losing time. Most of all, she was losing the sense that she could ever feel safe again, and she was terrified that this was simply who she was now—a woman who cleaned instead of lived, who pushed away thoughts instead of thinking them, who saw danger in every human face.
